section.title: God's Righteous Judgment
section.sectionRationale: Having exposed the open rebellion of the pagan world in chapter 1, Paul now turns and points his finger at the respectable moralist who nods along in agreement. The very act of condemning others convicts the judge, for he does the same things. God's judgment is impartial and according to truth: He will repay each one according to his deeds, whether Jew or Greek. Even Gentiles who never had the written law show its work written on their hearts, so that no one is left with an excuse.
section.thesis: God judges every person righteously, impartially, and according to what they have actually done; therefore the moralist who condemns others while practicing the same sins is not exempt but doubly guilty, and the whole human race, with the law written either on stone or on the heart, stands accountable before Him.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the self-condemning judge who has no excuse; God repaying each according to his deeds without favoritism; and the coming day when God judges the secrets of all, Jew and Gentile alike, doers rather than hearers being declared righteous.

units.label: No excuse for the one who judges
units.note: the judge condemned by his own verdict

verses.text: You, therefore, have no excuse, you who {{krino|pass judgment}} on another. For on whatever grounds you judge the other, you are condemning yourself, because you who pass judgment do the same things.
And we know that God's {{krima|judgment}} against those who do such things is based on truth.
So when you, O man, pass judgment on others, yet do the same things, do you think you will escape God's judgment?
Or do you disregard the riches of His kindness, tolerance, and patience, not realizing that God's kindness leads you to {{metanoia|repentance}}?
But because of your hard and unrepentant heart, you are storing up wrath against yourself for the day of wrath, when God's {{dikaiokrisia|righteous judgment}} will be revealed.

units.label: God will repay each according to his deeds
units.note: impartial judgment, first for the Jew, then for the Greek

verses.text: God “will repay each one according to his deeds.”
To those who by perseverance in doing good seek glory, honor, and immortality, He will give eternal life.
But for those who are self-seeking and who reject the truth and follow wickedness, there will be wrath and anger.
There will be trouble and distress for every human being who does evil, first for the Jew, then for the Greek;
but glory, honor, and peace for everyone who does good, first for the Jew, then for the Greek.
For God does not show favoritism.

units.label: Doers, not hearers; the law written on the heart
units.note: the day God judges the secrets of all through Christ

verses.text: All who sin apart from the law will also perish apart from the law, and all who sin under the law will be judged by the law.
For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but it is the doers of the law who will be declared righteous.
Indeed, when Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature what the law requires, they are a law to themselves, even though they do not have the law.
So they show that the work of the law is written on their hearts, their {{syneidesis|consciences}} also bearing witness, and their thoughts either accusing or defending them
on the day when God will judge men's secrets through Christ Jesus, as proclaimed by my gospel.

krino.gloss: To judge, to pass sentence, to condemn. Paul uses the verb against the moralist who sets himself up as a judge over others. The irony is that by his own standard he pronounces his own guilt, for he does the very things he condemns. To judge another is to publish the law by which you yourself will be measured.

krima.gloss: The verdict or sentence, the result of judging. God's krima is grounded in truth, not appearance; He sees what is really done and pronounces accordingly. Unlike human judgment, which is partial and often hypocritical, God's sentence is perfectly accurate and cannot be escaped.

metanoia.gloss: A change of mind that turns the whole person around, a turning from sin to God. God's kindness, tolerance, and patience are not indifference to sin but a summons; they are meant to lead the sinner to repentance. To despise that kindness by presuming on it is to store up wrath instead.

dikaiokrisia.gloss: Righteous judgment, a compound of righteousness and judgment. The day of wrath will reveal not arbitrary anger but God's perfectly just verdict. This word guards the character of God: His condemnation of sin is the fair and holy act of a righteous Judge, and it vindicates rather than tarnishes His name.

syneidesis.gloss: Conscience, the inner witness that knows with itself and testifies to right and wrong. Even Gentiles who never received the written law carry its work on their hearts, and their conscience either accuses or defends them. This inner court proves that all people have moral knowledge and so are without excuse before God.

basic.context: In chapter 1 Paul described humanity in open rebellion, suppressing the truth and given over to sin. A reader could easily agree and feel superior: those people deserve judgment. Chapter 2 turns to that reader. The one who condemns others, the moralist, the religious person who knows better, is caught in the same net, because he does the same things while claiming the moral high ground. Paul is closing every escape route so that grace can be received.
basic.hermeneutics: Read this as a courtroom scene. Paul uses a common ancient style called diatribe, arguing with an imagined objector, so the you here is a representative moralist, and by chapter 2 verse 17 clearly the Jew who trusts in the law. The point is not that anyone actually earns salvation by works, but that God's standard is impartial and real: He judges by deeds, according to truth, without favoritism. This exposes the moralist as guilty.
basic.originalLanguages: The passage turns on the language of judging. To krino others is to invite God's krima, His verdict, which is based on truth. God's kindness aims at metanoia, a real turning, not presumption. The day of wrath reveals His dikaiokrisia, righteous judgment. And even those without the written law have the work of the law on their hearts, their syneidesis, their conscience, accusing or defending them.
basic.typology: The day of wrath, when God's righteous judgment is revealed, echoes the prophetic day of the LORD, now focused on Christ Jesus as the appointed Judge. The law written on Gentile hearts anticipates the new covenant promise of the law written within, though here it functions to convict rather than to save.
basic.christ: The passage ends with the day when God judges the secrets of all through Christ Jesus. The Judge of all the earth is Jesus. This warning drives us to Him not only as Judge but as the only Savior, for if God repays each according to his deeds, and none of us can stand, then our one hope is the righteousness that comes as a gift in Christ, unfolded from chapter 3 onward.
basic.god: God is impartial, patient, and righteous. He shows no favoritism; He judges by truth and by deeds, not by ancestry or profession. His kindness is real and is meant to lead to repentance, yet He will by no means clear the guilty who presume upon it. This is a God whose judgment is trustworthy precisely because it is just.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 62:12 and Proverbs 24:12 declare that God repays each according to his work. Matthew 7:1-2 warns that with the judgment you pronounce you will be judged. 2 Chronicles 19:7 and Acts 10:34 affirm that God shows no partiality. Jeremiah 31:33 promises the law written on the heart, fulfilled in the new covenant.
basic.oneStory: From the beginning God has been the righteous Judge of all the earth. Here Paul shows that no one, not the pagan of chapter 1 nor the moralist of chapter 2, can stand before that judgment on the basis of their deeds. This shuts every mouth and prepares the way for the good news that a righteousness from God is coming, apart from works, for all who believe.

context.literary:
Romans 2:1 begins with 'therefore,' and the connection is a trap sprung on the reader. Chapter 1 ended with a catalog of the worst of the pagan world and a verdict, and a reader who agrees with it is exactly the person Paul now addresses. The shift of pronoun from 'they' to 'you' is the hinge of the whole section. For sixteen verses Paul never names the person addressed, and not until verse 17 does he say 'Jew.' The unnamed 'you' lets every reader step into the chair before discovering whose chair it is.

The passage has a clear shape. Verses 1 to 5 are a direct address in the style of the ancient diatribe, in which a teacher argues with an imagined objector and puts the objector's thoughts into sharp questions: 'do you think you will escape,' 'do you disregard the riches of His kindness.' Verses 6 to 11 state the principle of judgment. Paul builds it in parallel and then in chiasm: verse 6 gives the principle, verses 7 and 8 describe two outcomes, verses 9 and 10 repeat them in reverse order (trouble first, then glory), and verse 11 closes with 'God does not show favoritism.' Verses 12 to 16 then widen the principle to the two groups it covers, those with the law and those without it, ending with the day of judgment.

Two phrases frame the whole. 'First for the Jew, then for the Greek' appears twice, in verses 9 and 10, and echoes 1:16, where the same order described the gospel's power. Paul takes the order of privilege and applies it to judgment. Those who received the word first are held first to what it says.

Verse 16 closes the passage with the judge named: 'through Christ Jesus, as proclaimed by my gospel.' The section that began with a human judge ends with the divine one, and the gospel is already in view, which is why the section does not feel like pure law.
context.historical:
The Roman church included many Jewish Christians, back in the city after the emperor Claudius's expulsion of Jews, Acts 18:2, and they stood beside Gentile believers who had never known the law. Paul addresses a debate that was live in both groups. A Jewish reader of the period could hold a confident view of Israel's standing: Abraham was their father, the law was theirs, and God's patience with Israel was proof of His favor. John the Baptist had to warn people against saying 'We have Abraham as our father,' Matthew 3:9, and in John 8:33 the claim is repeated. The Wisdom of Solomon, a Jewish writing of the period, praises God because He overlooks sins that people may repent, and it speaks of His patience with Israel as a sign that Israel belongs to Him. Paul takes that very assurance and turns it: God's patience is meant to lead to repentance, not to presume.

The other half of the argument depended on common understandings in the Greek and Roman world. Educated Gentiles spoke of a moral law known to all through reason or nature, and everyone knew that even people who had never heard of Moses condemned murder and theft and honored their parents. Paul uses that widely shared idea in verses 14 and 15 without claiming that pagan morality is good enough. His point is that the existence of conscience proves that everyone has a standard and fails it.

The courtroom language also fit the setting. Roman citizens lived under a legal system in which judges, accusations and defenses were familiar. In verse 15 the conscience 'bears witness' and the thoughts 'accuse or defend,' as in a trial where the witness and the advocates are inside the person. Paul writes from Corinth, where he had himself stood before a Roman governor's judgment seat, Acts 18:12-17, and he would have felt the weight of the phrase 'the day when God will judge men's secrets' in a world that knew what it was to stand before a magistrate.
context.canonical:
The principle of verse 6 is quoted from the Old Testament: 'You will repay each one according to his deeds,' Psalm 62:12, and the similar words of Proverbs 24:12. The point that God does not show favoritism is a longstanding Old Testament teaching: He 'shows no partiality and accepts no bribe,' Deuteronomy 10:17, and Jehoshaphat tells the judges that the LORD 'shows no injustice or partiality,' 2 Chronicles 19:7. Paul is not inventing a new principle. He is reminding the Jew of what his own Scripture says about the God who judges.

The scene of verse 1 has a famous Old Testament model. When Nathan told David the story of the rich man who took a poor man's lamb, David burned with anger and condemned the man, and Nathan said, 'You are that man!' 2 Samuel 12:5-7. Paul's moralist is David before the prophet's finger.

God's patience, verse 4, quotes the oldest description of Himself that Israel knew, 'compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion,' Exodus 34:6. Jonah quotes the line as a complaint, because God's patience spared a city he wanted judged, Jonah 4:2. The danger Paul names is that the same truth can harden or soften depending on how it is received.

The promise that God would write His law on human hearts, Jeremiah 31:33, stands behind verses 14 and 15. The New Testament draws on the passage in many places. Jesus says the Father has given all judgment to the Son, John 5:22, and Paul preaches at Athens that God 'has set a day when He will judge the world with justice by the Man He has appointed,' Acts 17:31. Paul tells the Corinthians that 'we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ,' 2 Corinthians 5:10. The judge of the Old Testament, who 'will bring every deed into judgment, along with every hidden thing,' Ecclesiastes 12:14, is revealed in the New as Jesus, and it is the same judgment seen from two sides.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul writes to a church where Jews and Gentiles are learning to live as one body, and the first thing he must dismantle is the idea that anyone has a position from which to judge another. His target is not judging as such, since he will say in this very letter that rulers bear the sword to punish wrongdoing, Romans 13:4. His target is the habit of exempting oneself. The moralist says, in effect, 'God's judgment is for them, and I am safe because I know better, I belong to the right people, and God has been patient with me.' Paul wants each of those three supports knocked away.

The impartiality of God is the main weapon. Verses 6 to 11 say that the standard is the same for all and that the outcome depends on what a person does, not who he is. If Paul had stopped there, the reader would conclude that no one is safe, and that is exactly the conclusion he wants. By the time he reaches 3:9 and 3:20 he will say it plainly.

He also means the passage to be heard as an invitation. The kindness of verse 4 is not decoration. Paul begins with God's patience and ends with God's judgment so that the patience can be seen for what it is: a door left open. A reader who has taken the passage as a threat only has not noticed the question that sits at its centre, 'do you not realize that God's kindness leads you to repentance?'
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage describes the principle by which God will judge, and the judgment it describes is a fact about the final day, not an instruction about how to treat other people now. It does not tell believers to stop distinguishing right from wrong. Jesus told His disciples to stop judging in the sense of condemning, Matthew 7:1-2, and in the same chapter told them to 'beware of false prophets,' Matthew 7:15, which requires careful discernment. Paul himself asks, 'Are you not to judge those inside?' 1 Corinthians 5:12. What is forbidden is judgment from a position of imagined innocence.

The prescriptive part is the call that follows. If God's kindness is meant to lead to repentance, then every experience of His patience, every day free of consequences and every undeserved gift, is a summons. A believer should read his own comfort that way, and also the comfort of others. A good test is whether we treat another person's sin as a reason to look down or as a mirror, and whether our own freedom from judgment so far has made us humble or complacent.

The verses on 'doing good' in 2:7 and 2:10 are not a rule that works can earn eternal life. They describe the principle of judgment and the shape of a life that has been changed. The fuller account of how anyone gets there comes in 3:21-26 and chapter 4, and Paul does not expect the reader to read 2:7 apart from them.

debates.question: Does verse 13, 'the doers of the law will be declared righteous,' teach justification by works?

views.label: A hypothetical principle that no one meets
views.case: The classic Protestant reading holds that Paul states the standard of God's law as a standard in order to show that sinners fail it. Verse 20 of chapter 3 says no one will be justified by works of the law, and Galatians 3:10-12 says the law does not rest on faith. On this view the verse is a true principle that condemns the whole world.

views.label: A description of the justified, whose obedience is evidence
views.case: Others hold that Paul has in mind those who are justified by faith and then, by the Spirit, do what the law requires, Romans 8:4. Their deeds are the fruit that shows their standing, not its cause. Romans 2:26-29 and 'obedience that comes from faith,' Romans 1:5, point the same way.

views.label: A real standard at the final judgment applied to believers
views.case: Some argue that Paul means judgment according to works literally applies to everyone, believers included, and that their works are the public evidence of faith. This is how many read 2 Corinthians 5:10 and Matthew 25:31-46. Faith alone justifies, but faith is never alone.

debates.bearing: All three views agree that no one is saved by performance, and Paul does not leave the matter at 2:13. He is building a case, and the case is only complete when 3:20 says the law brings knowledge of sin and not justification.

debates.question: Who are the Gentiles who 'do by nature what the law requires,' verses 14 and 15?

views.label: Gentiles without the law who show a conscience
views.case: The older and most common reading takes these as ordinary non-Christian Gentiles whose conscience reflects the moral law. The word 'nature' and the phrase 'who do not have the law' suit this, and Paul's point is that even they have a standard and fall short of it. Calvin, and most of the Reformers, read it this way.

views.label: Gentile Christians
views.case: A reading going back to Augustine in his later writings, and held by many scholars today, takes the Gentiles as believers in whom the Spirit has written the law, Jeremiah 31:33. They support this with verse 29, where the Gentile is praised by God, and the language of doing the law in verses 26 and 27, which seems to describe real obedience.

views.label: A deliberately general category
views.case: Others suggest Paul does not mean to say how many do or whether they are saved. He states what happens whenever any Gentile acts rightly: it shows an inner law. He leaves open the question of how many, because his goal is to show the principle of impartial judgment.

debates.bearing: The context favors the first view, since Paul is still arguing that all are under sin and has not yet introduced the Spirit, but the second view takes seriously the force of 'written on their hearts.' Either way the passage does not teach that unbelieving Gentiles can be saved by their conscience, because Paul's conclusion in 3:9 is that all are under sin.

debates.question: Is the 'you' of verses 1 to 5 already the Jew?

views.label: A Jewish interlocutor from the start
views.case: The reference to 'riches of His kindness, tolerance, and patience' echoes Jewish teaching about God's patience with Israel, and verse 9 says 'first for the Jew.' Many scholars think Paul has the Jew in mind throughout, with the name held back until verse 17.

views.label: A representative moralist, Jewish or Gentile
views.case: Others note that the section opens with 'O man,' a general term, and that the Greek moral philosophers also condemned hypocrisy. On this view the 'you' is anyone who judges, and Paul narrows to the Jew in verse 17 because the Jew is the strongest example.

debates.bearing: The two views fit together. The 'you' begins as any moralist and becomes the Jew, the most obvious person to whom the description applies. The reader, whoever he is, is not allowed to leave the chair.

study.originalLanguages:
Paul's first sentence plays on one root. The one who 'passes judgment' is krinon, and the verdict he brings on himself is a krima, from the same family, and he asks in verse 3 whether he will 'escape' the krima of God. The verb that describes the moralist's act is the noun for the sentence that will fall on him. In verse 1 the phrase 'you are condemning yourself' translates katakrineis, a compound with a prefix that makes the verb mean to give a verdict against. The moralist is writing his own sentence.

The riches of God's kindness, verse 4, set a contrast with the treasure of wrath in verse 5. 'Do you disregard the riches' uses ploutos, and 'you are storing up wrath' uses thesaurizeis, literally 'you are treasuring up.' The same person who ignores one kind of treasure is quietly accumulating the other. The three words that describe God's goodness, chrestotes 'kindness,' anoche 'tolerance' or forbearance, and makrothymia 'patience,' belong together. The last is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for God's being 'slow to anger,' Exodus 34:6. Anoche, forbearance, returns in 3:25, where Paul says that in His forbearance God passed over the sins committed beforehand. The patience of 2:4 is being justified in 3:25 by the cross. The verb 'leads,' agei, is gentle: it describes drawing along, not forcing.

In verse 5 the 'hard and unrepentant heart' is sklerotes and ametanoeton kardian. 'Hard' recalls the stiff-necked, and 'unrepentant' is a negated form of metanoia, a change of mind. The word for 'righteous judgment,' dikaiokrisia, appears to be a compound of dikaios and krisis, uniting 'right' and 'verdict' in one word.

'Favoritism,' verse 11, is prosopolempsia, from the Hebrew idiom of 'lifting the face,' meaning to receive someone because of his appearance. The Hebrew idiom of showing partiality appears in Deuteronomy 10:17 and 2 Chronicles 19:7. The New Testament uses the compound repeatedly: Ephesians 6:9, Colossians 3:25 and James 2:1.

Verse 13 sets 'hearers,' akroatai, against 'doers,' poietai. The first word alludes to the Shema, 'Hear, O Israel,' Deuteronomy 6:4, the cry that defined a Jew as one who hears. James uses the same contrast in 1:22-25, and so does Jesus in the story of the two builders, Matthew 7:24-27. 'Declared righteous' is the verb dikaiothesontai, the legal verb of acquittal that will carry the whole of the letter.

In verse 14 the Gentiles are 'a law to themselves,' heautois eisin nomos, and in verse 15 'the work of the law' is singular, to ergon tou nomou. Paul does not say 'the works of the law.' He means the content or result of the law, the substance of its demand, and not a body of observances. The contrast matters when 3:20 speaks of 'works of the law' in the plural. Conscience, syneidesis, is literally 'knowing with oneself,' and 'bearing witness' is symmartyrousēs, 'bearing witness together.' The thoughts 'accusing' and 'defending' are courtroom words for prosecution and defense, so conscience sits as both. The word 'secrets,' krypta, in verse 16 returns in 2:29, where the true Jew is one 'in secret' (kryptō), so the judgment of the hidden and the praise of the hidden belong together.

typology.type: The prophetic day of the LORD, Amos 5:18-20
typology.fulfillment: The prophets warned a complacent Israel that the day they longed for would be darkness and not light, Amos 5:18, Zephaniah 1:14-15. Paul's 'day of wrath, when God's righteous judgment will be revealed,' verse 5, picks up exactly that tone, and he names the Judge. The day of the LORD is the day when God judges 'through Christ Jesus,' verse 16, and Acts 17:31 says He has fixed it. The escalation is that the Judge is also the Savior, so the day that brings terror to the unrepentant is the day believers long for, Philippians 3:20-21. The type is limited because Amos speaks of a nation in history, while Paul speaks of every person at the end.

typology.type: Nathan and David: the judge who is the guilty man, 2 Samuel 12:1-7
typology.fulfillment: David judged the rich man in the story and was told 'You are that man!' The moralist of Romans 2 is in the same position. David's response, 'I have sinned against the LORD,' 2 Samuel 12:13, and Psalm 51, shows what repentance looks like when God's kindness brings a person to see himself. The type points to the way the Gospel handles every case: the finger of the prophet becomes the finger of the Spirit, and the verdict is followed by forgiveness. It falls short because David was forgiven by a promise anticipating Christ, while Paul will show how the forgiveness is grounded in His blood.

typology.type: The law written on the heart, Jeremiah 31:33
typology.fulfillment: God promised that in the new covenant He would write His law on hearts. Paul says the Gentiles show the 'work of the law' written on their hearts, verse 15, and later says that what the law could not do, God has done by sending His Son, so that 'the righteous standard of the law might be fulfilled in us, who do not walk according to the flesh but according to the Spirit,' Romans 8:3-4. The correspondence is not exact: in chapter 2 the inner law convicts, and in the new covenant it empowers. The type shows that God always meant the law to reach the heart, and that is the work of the Spirit, 2 Corinthians 3:3.

typology.type: Abraham's question, 'Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?' Genesis 18:25
typology.fulfillment: Abraham appealed to the character of the Judge, and Paul does the same: God's judgment is 'based on truth,' verse 2. Abraham's concern was the righteous who might be swept up with the wicked. The question for Paul is who the righteous are, and the answer from Romans 3:10 is that none are. The escalation comes at the cross, where the Judge sentences His own Son so as to be 'just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus,' Romans 3:26. The type shows that God's justice is not a threat to the innocent but the guarantee that nothing wrong is overlooked.

study.christ:
The passage names Christ only once, in its last verse, and the placement is the point. The judgment of all hidden things happens 'through Christ Jesus,' verse 16. Jesus Himself said the Father 'has assigned all judgment to the Son,' John 5:22, and Peter told Cornelius that Jesus 'is the One appointed by God to judge the living and the dead,' Acts 10:42. The judge whose righteous verdict has been described is the One who came in the flesh and walked through the world, so His judgment is neither remote nor alien. He knows what is in man, John 2:25, and He has been 'tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin,' Hebrews 4:15.

The passage leads to Christ by forcing a question that only He can answer. If God repays each one according to his deeds and has no favorites, who will stand? The answer Paul gives starting at 3:21 is that the righteousness required has been supplied. The patience in verse 4 is explained at the cross, since 3:25 says God 'in His forbearance' passed over sins beforehand and then demonstrated His righteousness by presenting Christ as the atoning sacrifice. Without the cross, the patience of God would look like indifference. With it, God's forbearance is revealed as a deferred payment that He Himself made.

Christ is also the true doer of the law. In verse 13 the doers are declared righteous, and no one but Christ fits the description. He 'fulfilled all righteousness,' Matthew 3:15, and is 'the end of the law, to bring righteousness to everyone who believes,' Romans 10:4. The one who keeps the law perfectly takes the place of those who do not, and the benefits of His obedience are counted to them, 'through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous,' Romans 5:19. When Jesus says that whoever believes 'will not come under judgment,' John 5:24, He is not saying the standard has been lowered. He is saying the Judge has Himself taken the sentence.

The heart is a place where Christ works as well. The moralist has a hard and unrepentant heart, verse 5, and the promise is that God will give 'a new heart,' Ezekiel 36:26. Jesus is the one who changes it, as in the case of Zacchaeus, Luke 19:1-10, who began as a man who took more than he should and ended by repaying fourfold.

The hearers who do not do also find their reflection in the final words of the Sermon on the Mount, Matthew 7:24-27. The wise man builds on rock, and that rock is the One who speaks. A caution is needed: the passage does not directly teach the cross, and it should not be treated as if it does. It prepares for the cross by taking away every excuse, and by showing that the Judge is Christ Jesus. When Paul introduces the gift in 3:24 as 'freely by His grace,' the ground has been cleared by this chapter.
study.god:
The God of this passage is first of all a Judge whose verdicts are 'based on truth,' verse 2. That phrase says that His judgment does not depend on rumor, status or the cleverness of the defense. He sees what is hidden, which is why the passage ends with the 'secrets' of men. Samuel learned that 'man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart,' 1 Samuel 16:7, and Paul's argument depends on that kind of knowledge. The verdict is not a guess, because the Judge knows both the act and the motive.

He is impartial. 'God does not show favoritism,' verse 11, is one of the clearest statements of His character in the passage, and it cuts in two directions. Nobody is condemned because of the wrong birth, and nobody is excused because of the right one. Impartiality is good news for the poor and powerless, because there is no court in which a powerful person can buy a better result, Deuteronomy 10:17-18. It is bad news for the self-righteous, because they cannot rely on their record.

He is rich in kindness, tolerance and patience. Paul does not describe a judge who relishes punishment. The first thing he says about God's relation to the sinner is that He has been kind. The patience of God is not softness, and it is not unconditional. It has a purpose, 'repentance,' and a limit, 'the day of wrath.' Peter says the Lord is patient 'not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance,' 2 Peter 3:9. The God who sets a day is also the God who delays the day to give time.

He does not need to make an exception to be merciful. The principle of verses 6 to 11 is a statement of strict justice, and Paul does not weaken it. He lets the tension stand until the cross resolves it, where God shows Himself 'just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus,' Romans 3:26. This is one of the deepest things about the God of the Bible. He does not choose between righteousness and mercy.

He writes His law on hearts. The Gentiles, who had no Scripture, still show 'the work of the law' written on their hearts, verse 15. This means the moral order they know is no accident. It comes from a God who has made human beings in such a way that they know right from wrong, and who holds them to it.

For worship, this passage teaches reverence before a Judge who cannot be flattered, and gratitude for a patience that can be mistaken for silence. Praise belongs to the God who delays in order to rescue. A congregation that has heard Romans 2 sings the mercies of God more soberly and more gladly.

crossReferences.note: David is outraged by Nathan's story of the rich man who stole a poor man's lamb, and Nathan tells him, 'You are that man!' It is the exact movement of Romans 2:1: the person who judges a sin with indignation finds that he is the one it describes.

God describes Himself as compassionate, gracious and slow to anger. Paul's three words for God's goodness, kindness, tolerance and patience, rest on this self description, and the next verse in Exodus adds that He does not leave the guilty unpunished, which is the other half of Romans 2.

The psalm ends by saying God repays each one according to his deeds, and Paul quotes it in verse 6. The line follows a statement of God's strength and steadfast love, so the repayment is set in a context of God's faithfulness, not arbitrary power.

The proverb answers the excuse that one did not know. God weighs the heart and will repay each person according to his deeds. It supports the claim of Romans 2:16 that God judges secrets, and it closes off the plea of ignorance.

The LORD your God is God of gods and Lord of lords, who shows no partiality and accepts no bribe. This is the Old Testament source of verse 11, and it shows that impartiality is not a New Testament softening but the foundation of Israel's confession.

Jehoshaphat tells Judah's judges to act carefully, since the LORD their God shows no injustice, partiality or bribery. Paul's principle is one Israel taught its own magistrates, which makes it harder for a Jew to hear it as foreign.

Jesus says the measure you use will be measured to you. Paul gives the same warning in the language of the lawcourt, and he sees how it works: the standard we apply to others becomes the standard for ourselves.

Peter says God shows no favoritism but accepts those from every nation who fear Him and do what is right. This is Romans 2:11 spoken at the moment the gospel crosses to Gentiles, and it shows impartiality as both a warning and an open door.

God promises to put His law within His people and write it on their hearts. The Gentiles of Romans 2:15 show something of the same inner law, but the new covenant promise is of a law that enables obedience, not only one that accuses.

The Lord is patient, not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance. It is Romans 2:4 in another apostle's words, and it explains why God's judgment seems delayed: the delay is itself an act of kindness.

God will bring every deed into judgment, along with every hidden thing, whether good or evil. This is the Old Testament background of Romans 2:16, and it makes the judgment of secrets not a New Testament addition but the end of the wisdom tradition.

Paul says God overlooked the ignorance of earlier times and now commands all people to repent, because He has set a day to judge the world by the Man He appointed. It is Romans 2:4-16 compressed into a sermon and addressed to Gentiles, with the resurrection as the proof.

study.oneStory:
The Bible opens with a Judge, though we do not at first call Him that. In Genesis 3 He walks in the garden, asks questions and pronounces sentences. In Genesis 18:25 Abraham calls Him 'the Judge of all the earth,' and in the days of the flood and the fire on Sodom the Bible shows the Judge acting. The moral order of the world is not an accident. The universe is the realm of a God who sees and settles.

Romans 2 stands in the middle of the argument that this Judge must be reckoned with by everyone. Paul has shown the pagan world given over to its sins in chapter 1, and now he shows that the religiously respectable are in the same condition. The history of Israel supports him. The nation that received the law repeatedly broke it, and the prophets announced that the day of the LORD would fall on them first. Amos told a self-assured people that the day they longed for would be darkness, Amos 5:18-20. Paul's phrase 'first for the Jew, then for the Greek' gives the same order of accountability.

Yet the same story contains the patience of God. God 'waited patiently in the days of Noah while the ark was being built,' 1 Peter 3:20, Nineveh was spared when it repented, Jonah 3:10, and Israel was carried through generation after generation of exile and return. Romans 2:4 is the summary of that long history: His kindness is meant to lead to repentance. The cross is the place where patience and justice meet, Romans 3:25-26.

After the cross the two themes continue. The church is told to live as people who will give an account, 2 Corinthians 5:10, and also as people who have already been declared righteous, Romans 5:1. Hebrews says it is appointed for people to die once and after that to face judgment, and Christ will appear a second time 'not to bear sin, but to bring salvation to those who eagerly await Him,' Hebrews 9:27-28.

The new creation brings the day of verse 16 to its end. Revelation 20:11-15 describes the books opened and the dead judged 'according to their deeds,' using the same principle as Romans 2:6. In the same book those whose names are in the Lamb's book of life are spared, Revelation 21:27. The Judge who sees the secrets of every heart is also the Lamb on the throne, Revelation 5:6 and 22:1. Then 'He will wipe away every tear from their eyes,' Revelation 21:4, and the justice that was once feared becomes the ground of lasting peace. Romans 2 is the part of that story in which the Judge has not yet revealed the Savior, and so it is the part in which every reader must hear the verdict before the verdict is answered.

quiz.q: Why does the person who passes judgment on others have no excuse?

options.text: Because he does the same things he condemns, so his own verdict falls on himself.
options.note: Paul's point exactly: the judge condemns himself because he practices what he judges.

options.text: Because judging others is always forbidden under any circumstances.
options.note: Close, but Paul's issue is hypocrisy in judging, not that all moral discernment is wrong.

options.text: Because only God is allowed to have opinions about right and wrong.
options.note: God alone is the final Judge, but Paul's concern here is the hypocrite who does the same things.

options.text: Because the moralist has never sinned and so cannot relate.
options.note: The opposite is true; he is guilty of the very sins he condemns.

quiz.q: What is God's kindness, tolerance, and patience meant to lead a person to?

options.text: Repentance, a real turning from sin to God.
options.note: Verse 4 says plainly that God's kindness leads you to repentance.

options.text: A softened, grateful heart that begins to hate its sin.
options.note: A right response, and part of repentance, though Paul names the turning itself as the goal.

options.text: Confidence that God will overlook sin because He is patient.
options.note: That is presumption; Paul warns it stores up wrath rather than securing pardon.

options.text: Permission to keep sinning since judgment is delayed.
options.note: This despises the riches of His kindness and hardens the heart.

quiz.q: On what basis will God judge, according to this passage?

options.text: Impartially, according to truth and according to each person's deeds.
options.note: God repays each according to his deeds and shows no favoritism.

options.text: According to a person's actual conduct, weighed without partiality.
options.note: Right in substance; the fuller answer names both truth and impartiality.

options.text: According to whether a person possessed the written law of Moses.
options.note: Having the law is not the standard; doing it is, and both Jew and Gentile are judged justly.

options.text: According to a person's ancestry and religious standing.
options.note: God shows no favoritism; pedigree and profession give no exemption.

quiz.q: What does Paul say about the Gentiles who do not have the written law?

options.text: The work of the law is written on their hearts, and their conscience accuses or defends them.
options.note: Verses 14 and 15 exactly: they show the law's work within, with conscience bearing witness.

options.text: They carry an inner moral witness that leaves them accountable to God.
options.note: True and well stated, though it omits the specific mention of conscience accusing or defending.

options.text: They are automatically innocent because they never received the law.
options.note: The reverse; the law on the heart means they too are without excuse.

options.text: They have no moral knowledge of any kind.
options.note: Paul says the opposite: the work of the law is written on their hearts.

quiz.q: Through whom will God judge the secrets of all people?

options.text: Through Christ Jesus, as proclaimed by Paul's gospel.
options.note: Verse 16 names Christ Jesus as the one through whom God judges the secrets of all.

options.text: Through the risen Lord Jesus, appointed as Judge of all.
options.note: Correct in substance; the text specifically ties this to the gospel Paul preaches.

options.text: Through the law of Moses applied to every nation.
options.note: The law exposes sin, but the Judge on that day is Christ, not the law itself.

options.text: Through each person's own conscience acting alone.
options.note: Conscience bears witness, but the Judge is Christ Jesus, not the conscience.

questions: Paul says the one who judges others often does the same things. Where are you quickest to condemn in others a fault you tolerate in yourself?
God's kindness, tolerance, and patience are meant to lead to repentance. Have you been reading God's patience as approval, and how might you respond to His kindness as the summons it really is?

God judges impartially, according to deeds and according to truth. How does the certainty of a perfectly just Judge unsettle any confidence you place in your background, reputation, or religious record?
Conscience accuses or defends even those without the written law. When your conscience accuses you, do you silence it or bring it to Christ?
God will judge the secrets of all through Christ Jesus. How does knowing that your hidden life is fully seen, yet that the Judge is also the Savior, change the way you live this week?

translationNotes.note: God will repay each one according to his deeds quotes Psalm 62:12 and echoes Proverbs 24:12. Paul states the principle of judgment by works to establish accountability, not to teach a way of earning salvation, as 3:20 makes clear.

The doers of the law who will be declared righteous states the true standard of judgment. In the flow of the argument it exposes that no fallen person meets it, since 3:20 concludes that by works of the law no one will be justified.
Some manuscripts read through Jesus Christ. The verse rounds off the section by naming Christ as the one through whom God judges the secrets of all, tying final judgment to the gospel Paul preaches.
